samples: This program reads a text file (the one named on the command line, or `data/sample.txt` if none is given), lower-cases the words, counts how often each occurs, and prints the ten most frequent, each with its count. It splits words only on spaces and does not strip punctuation, so "word," and "word" would be counted separately, and the order of words with equal counts is not specified. It needs console, environment and file-read access, fails with a file error if the file can't be read, and I'm not sure its grouping step compiles as written, since that step has no `collect` or `sum` clause, which the cheat sheet always shows.

This program reads a text file, whose path is given as the first command-line argument (it falls back to a sample file in a data folder if none is given), and prints the ten most frequent words, each with its count right-aligned beside it. Words are lower-cased and split only on spaces and line breaks, so punctuation stays attached ("word," and "word" count separately), and the order of words with equal counts isn't specified. It needs console, environment and read-only file access, and it fails with a file error if the file can't be read.

This program reads a text file (the path comes from the first command-line argument, defaulting to a sample file), lowercases the words, counts how often each occurs, and prints the ten most frequent, one per line with the count right-aligned beside the word. It needs console, environment and read-only filesystem access, and it fails with a file error if the file can't be read. Words are split only on spaces, so punctuation stays attached ("word," and "word" count separately) and tabs aren't treated as separators. The grouping step also seems to lack the collect or sum clause that the language reference shows for grouped queries, so check that it compiles before relying on it.

This program reads a text file, whose path is the first command-line argument or a built-in sample file if none is given, and counts how often each word appears. It lower-cases the words, splits them on spaces only, and prints the ten most frequent ones with their counts, most frequent first. Punctuation stays attached to words, so "end." and "end" count separately; it needs console, environment and file-read access, and it fails with a file error if the file can't be read.

This program reads a text file, whose path is the first command-line argument or a built-in sample path if none is given. It lower-cases the words, counts how often each appears, and prints the ten most frequent, one per line with the count right-aligned beside the word. Words are split only on spaces within each line, so punctuation stays attached (a word followed by a comma counts separately from the bare word) and tabs are not treated as separators; it needs console, environment and file-read access, and it fails with a file error if the file can't be read. One caveat: the grouping step has no `collect` or `sum` after `group by`, a form the language reference doesn't show, so check that it compiles and behaves as intended before relying on it.
